phases.message: I'm Lucia Ferreira. This is my mail: notices and offers from two airlines and my travel agency, and a reply I sent. Read every message. Don't do anything yet: I'll send you to my card and then to each place that holds a credit of mine.
This is my Cardhollow card. Read its note and my statement, every page. Don't do anything yet.
This is Aerolark. Read its refund rules, and my credits and fees on every page. Ask for a refund of each item where the rule says one is owed, with the reason. Leave alone what is not owed.
This is Skylindle, my second airline. Do the same here: read its rules and my credits on every page, and ask for the refunds that are owed.
This is Tripcairn, my travel agency. Do the same here. Then tell me, across all three, what you asked to be refunded and why, what you left alone and why, and what I should get back.

aer_rules.text: Aerolark refund rules (invented). Today is Friday 9 October 2026. Topics: index, change, refund, credit, fees, time. These are the airline's own summary of the Department of Transportation's refund rule, 14 CFR Part 260. Read your credits with read_credits.

A significant change. A flight is significantly delayed or changed when it leaves or lands 3 hours or more later or earlier than scheduled on a domestic itinerary, or 6 hours or more on an international one; or it leaves from or lands at a different airport; or it has more connection points; or the passenger is downgraded to a lower class of service. A different connecting airport counts only for a passenger with a disability. A smaller time change is not a significant change.

When a refund is owed. A passenger holding a nonrefundable ticket for a flight the airline cancelled, or significantly delayed or changed, who declines the new flight, the rebooking and any compensation, is owed a full refund of the fare, taxes and fees. The airline should pay it without being asked; where it has left a credit or nothing instead, the passenger asks and the refund is then due within the time below. A refund is not owed for a flight the passenger cancelled or changed herself.

Credits. An airline may offer a voucher or credit instead of a refund only if it states the passenger's right to a refund, and the passenger affirmatively accepts it. A credit the airline issues on its own, which the passenger has not accepted, leaves the refund owed. A credit the passenger chose, in writing, is a choice, and the refund is not owed. A credit already refunded, or already spent, cannot be refunded again.

Fees. A fee paid for a service the airline did not provide, through no fault of the passenger, such as a seat the aircraft does not have, is refunded automatically. A fee for a flight the passenger cancelled herself is not.

How and when. A refund goes back in the original form of payment, within 7 business days of the request for a card purchase and within 20 calendar days for other payments. No processing fee may be kept. Ask with request_refund, one item at a time.

What is covered. The refund rule covers a scheduled flight to, from or within the United States. A flight between two points outside the United States, such as Dublin and Lisbon, is not covered by it, whatever the airline.

tca_rules.text: Tripcairn travel agency (invented). Today is Friday 9 October 2026. Tripcairn charged your card for the tickets you bought through it, so it is the merchant of record and refunds what an airline says is owed. Topics: index, refunds. Read your credits with read_credits.

Refunds through Tripcairn. For a flight an airline cancelled or significantly changed (3 hours or more on a domestic itinerary, 6 hours or more on an international one, a different airport, more connections or a lower class of service), a passenger who declined it is owed a refund to the card within 7 business days of her request; a credit Tripcairn issued without her choice leaves the refund owed. A credit already spent is not refunded. Ask with request_refund.
